newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's overseas countries attack rice import quota.
newsitem.headline: EU's overseas countries attack rice import quota.

text.p: An extension of European Union safeguard measures against rice imports is unjustified, the Overseas Countries and Territories (OCT) Trade Association said on Friday.

The association, representing member states' overseas territories, was complaining after the European Commission on Wednesday set a new duty-free tariff quota of 69,610 tonnes from May 1 to September 30, 1997, to curb a sharp increase in rice imports.
It followed a limit of 44,278 tonnes from January 1 to April 30.

"The...Association strongly denies that OCT imports are having a negative impact on the interests of rice producers in the EU and ACP (African, Caribbean and Pacific) countries," it said in a statement.
The EU is a net rice importer of around 400,000 tonnes a year, of which only half is supplied by OCT countries, it said.
OCT countries do not produce or export japonica rice -- the variety most affected by the market crisis, it added.

An independent study by the Dutch economic institute NEI found that the crisis, which has depressed prices, was due to EU reforms agreed in December 1995 reducing market intervention and introducing more competition.

The association disputed a European Commission statement that imports of rice from the overseas countries surged to 365,029 tonnes in 1996 from 58,000 tonnes in 1992, saying that imports in 1996 were 212,417 tonnes.
The safeguard measures violated a 1991 agreement on the OCT, it said, adding that it was considering legal action.
The association urged the EU not to take similar action against imports of OCT sugar, which it said represented less than 0.1 percent of EU sugar production, or 5,000 tonnes annually.
Although there are plans to nearly double OCT sugar production capacity, it would still amount to only 150,000 tonnes, or 0.9 percent of EU output.
